extracted.intended_audience: regulated electric utilities and independent power producers, environmental consultants and engineers, state regulators, attorneys, and public commenters on EPA CCR rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble and regulatory text explaining EPA's risk findings, modeling approaches, definitions, and the finalized regulatory requirements for legacy coal combustion residual (CCR) surface impoundments and CCR management units (CCRMU). Includes numeric risk thresholds, constituent priorities, and provisions for compliance and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a “Legacy CCR Surface Impoundment”
rubrics_metrics.description: A legacy CCR surface impoundment must meet three criteria: (1) The unit meets the definition of a CCR surface impoundment; (2) The unit contains both CCR and liquids on or after October 19, 2015; and (3) The unit is located at an inactive electric utility or independent power producer. This definition is codified in § 257.53.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three criteria must be met for a unit to be a legacy CCR surface impoundment; the date-of-applicability (October 19, 2015) is used to restore the status quo consistent with the USWAG decision and is considered the most protective option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory risk thresholds (section 4004(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers risks that warrant regulation as cancer risks greater than 1 × 10^−5 and non-cancer risks exceeding a hazard quotient (HQ) of 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these numeric benchmarks to determine whether modeled or measured risks from leakage or exposure pathways fall within the range that typically justifies regulatory controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituents prioritized for further evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 assessment identifies arsenic, lithium, molybdenum, and thallium as constituents that warranted further evaluation; these were found in the 2014 Risk Assessment to pose the greatest risk for unlined surface impoundments and have the greatest demonstrated potential to spread and pose risk on a national scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constituents serve as reasonable screens/risk drivers for modeling and monitoring of groundwater impacts from CCR units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and adequacy of engineered liners (modeling assumption validation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical facility reporting and liner demonstration documents indicate a higher prevalence of unlined impoundments than previously modeled (EPA earlier estimated 65% unlined impoundments; review of facility documents indicates closer to 83% have no engineered liner). Additionally, around 10% of landfills and surface impoundments with a composite liner have entered corrective action, suggesting liners may not perform as previously modeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling and risk conclusions should be updated based on facility-reported liner documentation and corrective-action status; do not assume previously modeled liner performance without verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of co-disposal with coal refuse on leaching behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-disposal of CCR with coal refuse (coal preparation wastes) can make the overall waste pH far more acidic, which increases solubility of multiple Appendix IV constituents and can drive higher leakage rates. Modeled cancer risks for co-disposal ranged up to 1 × 10^−3 for trivalent arsenic and 4 × 10^−4 for pentavalent arsenic; non-cancer HQs reached double-digit values for several constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for historical co-disposal practices (which were more common prior to ~1995) in risk modeling for older units; even if current co-disposal rates are low, legacy practices may meaningfully increase risk estimates for older units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disposal below the water table
rubrics_metrics.description: Disposal beneath the water table (continuous or intermittent) creates saturated conditions that increase leachate volumes, maintain hydraulic gradients that drive leachate away from units, can lead to long-lived leakage after closure, and can alter groundwater chemistry (reducing conditions) that mobilize some contaminants such as arsenic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling and monitoring must explicitly consider units that are or were in contact with groundwater; expect potentially higher contaminant transport and longer-lasting impacts. Removal of saturated ash may be the only reliable source control in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of redox conditions and limitations of standardized leaching tests (LEAF and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized leaching tests and LEAF data tend to reflect oxidizing conditions (due to atmospheric contact during sampling and analysis) and therefore may not capture elevated leachate concentrations that occur under reducing conditions found in saturated CCR. Field measurements under reducing conditions have shown porewater arsenic concentrations (e.g., 4,100 mg/L) far higher than LEAF or compiled porewater 90th percentiles used in prior modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When field conditions diverge from laboratory (oxidizing) conditions, incorporate geochemical speciation modeling and field data reflecting reducing conditions to avoid underestimating leakage and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling framework for CCRMU fills (two-model approach and benchmarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA used EPACMTP run at specified distances along plume centerlines to estimate releases and downgradient concentrations and then ran MODFLOW-USG on subsets to characterize full plume magnitude and extent. Groundwater concentrations modeled at the waste boundary were compared to Groundwater Protection Standards (GWPS) and concentrations at 500 and 1,000 feet were used to calculate risk to individual reasonably maximally exposed (RME) receptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of fate-and-transport (EPACMTP) and groundwater flow (MODFLOW-USG) models; compare modeled concentrations to GWPS and risk benchmarks and consider both fixed-location concentrations and full plume volume/time dynamics when drawing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative exceedance metrics for CCRMU fills
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeled 90th percentile groundwater concentrations at the waste boundary exceeded GWPS by factors of 26 for arsenic III, 19 for arsenic V, 156 for molybdenum, and 19 for thallium. MODFLOW-USG runs showed peak risks (e.g., arsenic V peak risk 1 × 10^−4 averaged over 32 million gallons; molybdenum peak exceedance of 10 averaged over 27 Mgal) and plume dissipation times on the order of centuries to millennia for some scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both factor-of-exceedance at the waste boundary and plume-scale metrics (peak risk, average risk, plume volume, time to dissipate) to assess potential for lasting and widespread groundwater impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for CCRMU fills to create environmentally significant plumes even at small placements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's sensitivity analysis found GWPS exceedances are possible for placements below 1,000 tons; model runs with placements ranging from ~3,500 to 70,000 tons over 0.15 to 2.0 acres produced plumes large enough to sustain residential exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume very small placements are benign; evaluate fills down to low tonnages and be cautious about extrapolating below available model runs because uncertainty increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil exposure pathways and thresholds for residential receptor scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated incidental ingestion of CCR-soil mixtures and direct exposure to gamma radiation. Radon emanation was generally lower than most soils and not retained. For gamma radiation, PRG-based modeling showed cancer risks at or above 1 × 10^−5 for 90th and 50th percentile activities with a 40 cm cover, and a 90th percentile activity produced a 1 × 10^−4 cancer risk with a 20 cm cover. Mixing thresholds for radionuclides to exceed 1 × 10^−4 cancer risk were >11% (90th percentile activity) and >21% (50th percentile activity). For arsenic, >33% mixing (90th percentile concentration) could produce cancer risk >1 × 10^−4; at 50th percentile arsenic concentration this risk would not occur at any degree of mixing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing soil risks from CCR fills, consider direct gamma exposure and incidental ingestion under likely cover thicknesses and plausible mixing percentages; account for percentile variability in activity/concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological soil risk drivers from CCR accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing incremental CCR contributions to ecological soil screening levels, antimony (for mammals), selenium (for plants and mammals), and vanadium (for birds) were identified as the constituents most likely to drive ecological risk and require further evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ecological benchmarks in addition to human-health benchmarks; some ecological benchmarks may be lower than typical background, but incremental increases from CCR can still pose actionable ecological risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unit size and its effect on national risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Although previously excluded (historical/inactive) units tend to be somewhat smaller on average (excluded units modeled average 77 acres for landfills and 28 acres for impoundments vs regulated 107 and 47 acres), there is substantial overlap in size ranges and no indication size differences of this magnitude notably affect national risk. Much of the facilities' geographic variability was already captured in prior modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare size distributions and ranges rather than means alone; overlapping ranges may mean small-to-moderate size differences do not translate to materially different national risk estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative and confounding effects from adjacent or upgradient legacy units
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple units located directly adjacent to one another increase the total leakage area and could produce greater cumulative offsite risk than predicted by modeling each unit individually. Legacy impoundments and CCRMU located upgradient of regulated units can confound background monitoring, potentially delaying or preventing detection and corrective action for regulated units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk assessments and monitoring programs should account for co-located units and the potential for legacy units to influence background groundwater quality; single-unit modeling may underestimate cumulative exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical surveys and facility reporting to inform modeling assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relied on multiple data sources (EPA Surveys, EPRI surveys, facility-specific liner demonstration documents, location restriction demonstrations) to re-evaluate prevalence of liners, historical co-disposal practices, and occurrences of disposal below the water table; these empirical data led to revisions in modeled assumptions and risk conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate facility-reported documents and historical surveys into updated risk models; do not rely solely on older national-scale assumptions when new facility data are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to regulatory requirements for legacy CCR surface impoundments
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is amending 40 CFR part 257, subpart D to require legacy CCR surface impoundments to comply with the same regulations that apply to inactive CCR impoundments at active facilities, except for the location restrictions (at §§ 257.60-257.64) and liner design criteria (at § 257.71). The Agency is also establishing new requirements specific to legacy CCR surface impoundments and new compliance deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legacy impoundments will be subject to most inactive-impoundment regulatory requirements; stakeholders should review the specified exceptions and new compliance deadlines in the final rule text.
